clinicalPearls: Patients typically present with abdominal pain or symptoms of maldigestion; pain is variable in location, severity, and frequency, may be constant or intermittent, and can be exacerbated by eating, leading to fear of eating and weight loss (p.2752).
There is often a disparity between the reported severity of abdominal pain and the physical findings, which mainly consist of nonfocal abdominal tenderness (p.2752).

In contrast to acute pancreatitis, serum amylase and lipase are usually NOT strikingly elevated in chronic pancreatitis; low serum pancreatic enzyme levels are moderately specific but have poor sensitivity (p.2752).
Cumulative prevalence of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency exceeds 80%; overt steatorrhea in a patient with chronic pancreatitis is highly suggestive of this complication (p.2752).
A random fecal elastase-1 level on a formed stool specimen can help confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in patients with milder symptoms (p.2752).

Diffuse calcifications on a plain abdominal film usually indicate significant pancreatic damage and are pathognomonic for chronic pancreatitis; tropical pancreatitis (often SPINK1-associated) characteristically shows bulky calcifications (p.2752).

Lifetime prevalence of chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes exceeds 80%; most develop hyperglycemia from insulin deficiency due to islet cell loss, but diabetic ketoacidosis, diabetic coma, and end-organ damage (retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy) are uncommon (p.2752).

Cigarette smoking is an independent, dose-dependent risk factor for chronic pancreatitis and recurrent acute pancreatitis; continued alcohol and smoking exposure are associated with disease progression including fibrosis and calcifications (p.2750).
Metabolic bone disease is highly prevalent, with about 65% of patients having osteopenia or osteoporosis (p.2752).
harrison.pathophysiology: Chronic pancreatitis is characterized by irreversible damage to the pancreas (in contrast to the reversible changes of acute pancreatitis), defined by histologic abnormalities including chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and progressive destruction (atrophy) of both exocrine and endocrine tissue. Irrespective of the mechanism of injury, pancreatic stellate cell activation leads to cytokine expression and production of extracellular matrix proteins contributing to inflammation and collagen deposition. Proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6) and oxidants induce stellate cell activity with new collagen synthesis; TGF-beta-mediated autocrine self-activation pathways may explain disease progression even after removal of noxious stimuli. Etiologies are framed by the TIGAR-O classification (Toxic-metabolic, Idiopathic, Genetic, Autoimmune, Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis, Obstructive). Heavy alcohol use is the most common clinically apparent cause in U.S. adults, though additional factors are required for disease development (not all heavy drinkers develop disease). Genetic predisposition (e.g., PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen mutations preventing destruction of prematurely activated trypsin; CFTR and SPINK1 disease modifiers) accounts for up to 15% of previously idiopathic cases. Cardinal manifestations are abdominal pain, steatorrhea, weight loss, diabetes mellitus, and, less commonly, pancreatic cancer (p.2750-2752).
additionalDifferentials: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (must be excluded on imaging)
Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1 AIP / IgG4-related disease; type 2 / idiopathic duct-centric)
nonInfectiousMimics: Pancreatic cancer (a poor response to glucocorticoids in suspected autoimmune pancreatitis should raise suspicion of pancreatic cancer)
Autoimmune pancreatitis (type 1 can mimic primary sclerosing cholangitis via IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis)
additionalInvestigations: Fecal elastase-1 (random level on a formed stool specimen) to confirm exocrine pancreatic insufficiency
Abdominal CT (initial imaging modality of choice) to show calcifications, dilated pancreatic/biliary ducts, atrophy, and to exclude pseudocyst and cancer
Endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS); five or more of nine endosonographic features considered diagnostic, though not specific for early disease
EUS with endoscopic pancreatic function testing (EUS-ePFT)
Direct pancreatic function test using secretin (best sensitivity; becomes abnormal when >=60% of exocrine function is lost)
Plain abdominal film for diffuse calcifications
Serum amylase/lipase (usually not strikingly elevated), serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (may indicate cholestasis from biliary stricture)
Serum IgG4 (supportive of type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis)
redFlags: Increased risk of pancreatic cancer: cumulative risk is 4% at 20 years after diagnosis of chronic calcific pancreatitis; hereditary PRSS1 and tropical pancreatitis carry an even higher risk than other forms.
Jaundice, cholestasis, and biliary cirrhosis from chronic inflammation around the intrapancreatic common bile duct.

Gastrointestinal bleeding from peptic ulceration, gastritis, a pseudocyst eroding into the duodenum, arterial bleeding into the pancreatic duct (hemosuccus pancreaticus), or ruptured varices from splenic vein thrombosis.
harrison.prognosis: Chronic pancreatitis is an irreversible disease; there are currently no therapies to reverse or delay disease progression, so management is focused on screening for and treating complications. Patients have impaired quality of life and significant morbidity with frequent health encounters. Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (cumulative prevalence >80%) and chronic pancreatitis-related diabetes (lifetime prevalence >80%) commonly develop. The 20-year cumulative risk of pancreatic cancer in chronic calcific pancreatitis is 4%, higher in hereditary PRSS1 and tropical forms (p.2752-2754).
pitfalls: Diagnosis of early or mild chronic pancreatitis is challenging because there is no accurate biomarker, and serum amylase/lipase are usually not strikingly elevated (unlike acute pancreatitis) (p.2752).
EUS is not specific enough to diagnose early chronic pancreatitis alone and may show positive features in patients with diabetes, a smoking history, or even normal aging individuals (p.2752).
Elevated serum IgG4 has a low positive predictive value for autoimmune pancreatitis when used in isolation from other clinical findings (p.2751).
Complete correction of steatorrhea with pancreatic enzyme replacement is uncommon, even though enzyme therapy usually controls diarrhea and improves fat absorption (p.2753).
Meta-analyses show no consistent benefit of enzyme therapy at reducing pain; any pain relief may reflect improvement of dyspepsia from maldigestion (p.2753).
harrison.severityClassification: Etiologic classification follows the TIGAR-O system: Toxic-metabolic (alcohol, tobacco smoking, hypercalcemia, hyperlipidemia/hypertriglyceridemia, chronic renal failure), Idiopathic (early onset, late onset, tropical), Genetic (PRSS1 cationic trypsinogen, CFTR, CASR, CTRC, SPINK1), Autoimmune (type 1 IgG4-related; type 2 idiopathic duct-centric), Recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis (postnecrotic, recurrent acute), and Obstructive (pancreas divisum, duct obstruction by tumor, preampullary duodenal wall cysts, posttraumatic duct strictures). Some genetic conditions are disease modifiers requiring additional factors to cause disease (p.2750).
